extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and mathematical researchers (readers of Hilbert's 1900 ICM lecture); historians of mathematics; those interested in research directions
extracted.subtask_description: Digitized text of David Hilbert's 1900 ICM lecture discussing the role of problems in mathematics and how surveying unsettled questions can indicate future directions for the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abundance of problems indicates vitality
rubrics_metrics.description: As long as a branch of science offers an abundance of problems, so long is it alive; a lack of problems foreshadows extinction or the cessation of independent development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert asserts that the presence of many open problems is a marker of a living, independently developing subfield; conversely a dearth of problems signals decline. Use the quantity and richness of open questions as a diagnostic for the health of a mathematical area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep significance of certain problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The deep significance of certain problems for the advance of mathematical science in general and the important role which they play in the work of the individual investigator are not to be denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise problems that have broad significance for the advancement of mathematics and that meaningfully influence an investigator's work. Such problems shape the field and justify concentrated effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems should test the investigator and foster new methods
rubrics_metrics.description: It is by the solution of problems that the investigator tests the temper of his steel; he finds new methods and new outlooks, and gains a wider and freer horizon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select or value problems that challenge researchers in ways that lead to methodological innovation and broader perspectives. A good problem is one that forces the development of new techniques and insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey unsettled questions to forecast progress
rubrics_metrics.description: If we would obtain an idea of the probable development of mathematical knowledge in the immediate future, we must let the unsettled questions pass before our minds and look over the problems which the science of today sets and whose solution we expect from the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To predict or guide future research directions, systematically review current open problems; the set of unsettled questions is a practical indicator of where advances are likely to occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical continuity: each age has its own problems
rubrics_metrics.description: History teaches the continuity of the development of science. We know that every age has its own problems, which the following age either solves or casts aside as profitless and replaces by new ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate problems with awareness of historical context: some problems will be resolved, others deemed unproductive and abandoned. Historical perspective helps judge which problems are likely to endure or lead to progress.
